question: A learning and development specialist has a Claude-drafted explanation of a new expenses process written for finance staff. She now needs a version for field engineers who never open the finance system. What should she do first?
options: A) Cut the draft down to roughly half its present length so that the field engineers will read it.
B) Ask Claude to simplify the wording of the existing text until it reads a good deal more easily.
C) Ask Claude to add a glossary explaining the finance terms that the draft already uses.
D) Work out what the field engineers actually have to do differently, and write to that.
correct_answers: D) Work out what the field engineers actually have to do differently, and write to that.
explanations: Halving the length is an arbitrary cut with no principle behind it, and it is as likely to remove the steps the engineers need as the ones they do not.

Simplifying the wording keeps the finance staff's version of the process and only changes its surface. The engineers would get an easier read of material that is still organised around someone else's job.
A glossary makes unfamiliar terminology survivable but leaves the engineers reading a finance-system walkthrough that mostly does not apply to them.

Correct. Adapting for an audience starts from what that audience needs to do, not from the existing text. Once she knows which parts of the process the engineers actually touch, the register, the length and the level of detail all follow from it.
